implementation_notes: Rust has no user-declared constructors and no classes, so the textbook poltergeist has no natural spelling — but `struct UserCreator(String)` plus `impl UserCreator { fn run(self) }` is exactly it, and the compiler gives no warning because the type is used. Rust's own idiom is a free function, and the `impl` block on the data type is where the behaviour belongs. The support level is discouraged because the type carries no invariant, no lifetime distinction and no trait: a struct with one field, one method and no trait implementation is pure ceremony, and the idiomatic replacement is shorter. The genuine exception is a builder with real configuration, which Rust models well.
idiom_name: one-shot struct; Rust has no reason for one
alternative: Delete the struct and call a free function that owns the behaviour; if the operation needs state, define a named struct with real methods and give it value semantics.
pitfalls: A newtype wrapping a single value is not a poltergeist — it is a typed identifier that the compiler enforces, and removing it loses type safety.
A tuple struct used as a builder with several fields is a legitimate builder.
`#[derive(Default)]` on a single-field poltergeist makes the unused field harder to notice.
